CausalChain: Radiotherapy modulates local tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) --> TIME remodeling leads to altered production of immunosuppressive factors (e.g., TGF-β1, IDO) in the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE) --> Elevated STIE factors drive T cell exhaustion and hinder neoantigen-specific T cell infiltration --> PD-1 blockade alone is insufficient under high immunosuppressive conditions --> Targeted inhibition of these STIE factors concurrently with optimized radiotherapy restores effective T cell responses and recruitment --> Enhanced anti-tumor immunity and improved immunotherapy outcomes.
Hypothesis: A combined therapeutic strategy that integrates optimized radiotherapy dosing to reshape the TIME with pharmacologic inhibition of key STIE immunosuppressive mediators (such as TGF-β1 and IDO) will reverse T cell exhaustion, increase neoantigen-specific T cell recruitment, and thereby overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade in solid tumors.
Abstract: The current review elucidates the complex interplay between the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) in the context of immunotherapy, radiotherapy, and combined treatment modalities. Evidence from recent single‐cell and spatial transcriptomic studies has revealed heterogeneous immunologic signatures that contribute to response variability to PD-1 blockade, including factors such as soluble TGF-β1, IDO activity, and the presence of exhausted or precursor T cell subpopulations. Building on this, we propose a novel integrated therapeutic approach that targets systemic immunosuppressive mediators while modulating local immune architectures to reinvigorate tumor-specific T cell responses. Here, we hypothesize that fine-tuning radiotherapy dosing to remodel TIME in parallel with selective inhibition of STIE-derived factors may reverse T cell exhaustion, promote neoantigen-specific T cell infiltration, and thereby enhance the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor immunotherapy.
